title: Roundtrip: Canonical completion + Shard/Lexeme Provenance
body:
Closes #2381
Closes #1792
Closes #2296
Subsumes #2079
References #2373 (known-outstanding)

## Goal: round-tripping

This PR makes every editor-reachable state round-trip: the buffer's segment parses to a term, and printing that term (segment-to-segment, via ExpToSegment) reproduces the original (tile ids, labels, shards, secondary) up to a small quotient described below. This is supported by property-based testing. Previously many states didn't survive the trip: incomplete tiles were dumped or dropped, quotes around labels and leading + in sum types disappeared, literal spellings normalized (007 -> 7, 4.0 -> 4.), unknown infix operators created multiholes which lost the operator string, etc.

This enables transforms on terms (eg refactorings, agent edits) while perserving all previously ephemeral editor state. The stacked refactorings PR is the first consumer.

The mechanism has two halves: canonical completion turns every incomplete segment into a well-formed one deterministically, and a small amount of lexical provenance recorded on terms lets the segment printer reconstruct exactly what the user had typed.

## Canonical completion

This assigns a canonical completion to every incomplete segment. Unlike the previous dump logic, canonical completions do not depend on caret position. However, ergonomic completions can't depend simply on
term structure: when inserting a new form, e.g. a let expression above existing code, term structure alone is ambiguous as to whether the new code wraps the code below or sits purely above it. The caret-based heuristic used previously is (a) only useful for incomplete forms in the caret segment, and (b) necessitates either re-completing on caret movement (expensive and potentially confusing) or a hidden history dependence (confusing).

The new heuristic is based on partitioning, meaning which following content an incomplete form absorbs. This is decided by indentation: after a linebreak, content at same-or-lesser indentation than the incomplete tile's line ends the partition. This subsumes the old, somewhat ugly "reset after a blank line" heuristic and is the intent-based discrimination discussed next.

Where the missing delimiters go — placement follows an evidence hierarchy (details in plans/completion-heuristics.md): a leftover prefix token (`i` for a deleted `in`, `-` for `->`) or the deletion's own junction debris pins the delimiter exactly where it was; only evidence-free states fall back to the structural defaults below. The engine completes ONE tile per pass (strongest evidence first, weak ties innermost-first) and recurses on the materialized result, so the suggestion set is a replay script: applying everything shown reproduces the computed result by construction, and jointly-broken forms (delete a case's `end` AND its let's `in`) restore compatibly.
- Missing closers are appended at the end of their partition, stopping before a span-final trailing operator when that strictly reduces synthesized holes (`test 1 == 1 end;` restores with the `end` before the `;`). A single-line form's closer glues back over a trailing linebreak (`let x = 1` + blank line + `2` takes its `in` on the definition line); a multiline form keeps its closer on its own line (a broken multiline case-def restores `end in` exactly where it was).
- Missing openers are placed at the start of their closer's left-operand span in the partition skel — the maximal span the completed form can absorb without crossing enclosing structure — bounded by line-walls: a deleted mid-program `let`/`if`/`case` head stays on its own line instead of absorbing the definitions above. So let a = 1,2] completes to let a = [1,2] in ?, not by hoisting [ above the let. Same-position ties open the later closer outermost: 1) + 2) -> ((1) + 2). Opener spans are also clamped by slot sort: a restored head lands at the nearest span that fits its interior slot (the second `let` of `let a = 1 in let b = 2 in b`, deleted inline, restores at `b` — a complete let can't be a pattern), while Exp-slot wrappers like a deleted `(` keep the maximal wrap.
- Missing middle delimiters (let x in 2, if true else 2; targeted put-down can strand an interior delimiter in the backpack) can't be appended like the others, because reassembly requires shard order. The tile is instead completed in place: each original child stays in the slot opened by its original left shard, and newly created slots get a hole, so let x in 2 completes to let x = ? in 2. The synthesized grout ids derive deterministically from surrounding tile ids, so completion is stable across recomputation.

## Indentation now user-owned

A non-obvious part of this design is that the indentation heuristic requires making indentation user-owned. This isn't
essential for round-tripping itself, but it's what makes canonical completion ergonomic, as well as resolveing a problem of its own.

Indentation around incomplete code has the same wrapping-uncertainty as completion, and on dev it leads to indentation thrashing: typing on one line causes lines below to indent and unindent repeatedly. So the row-indentation system is removed in favor of 'traditional' indentation: indentation is now simply regular whitespace (secondary), owned by the user.

Like conventional editors, we don't re-indent everything on every edit. Pressing enter inserts indentation after the new linebreak only, using the same indentation logic as before, so left-to-right entry gets the indentation you expect and nothing below the caret moves. **Cmd+S formats per a 4-level setting (none / indent / spaces / breaks; default respaces + re-indents); Cmd+Shift+S always pretty-prints.**

There is a nut menu setting, on by default, for limited auto-identation: Completing a delimiter re-indents the lines it affects. Settled (roughly: not containing incomplete tiles) regions get exact re-indentation; unsettled ones a uniform shift.

The presence of user-owned indentation is what allows intent-based discrimination: the completion only absorbs following lines if they are indented relative to the incomplete form's line. The user can indent/dedent to get the behavior they want, but in practice they don't have to, because the enter-inserted indentation suffices for the completion to do what you expect during left-to-right entry, whether writing new code or code above existing code.

The general principle is to move all history sensitivity into secondary, and all system history-dependence into auto-formatting behavior. The user has full control over secondary, so none of this is fundamentally hidden or out of their control. When the code is complete, autoformat erases any trace of historical dependence; it exists purely during incomplete states.

## What round-tripping adds data-structure-wise

Two new fields on the IdTag annotation:
- incomplete: list((Id.t, list(int))): for each canonically completed tile, which shards the user actually typed. The
printer strips synthesized shards on the way back out, so incomplete tiles survive the trip; MakeTerm threads the same masks so statics sees the completed form.
- lexeme: option(string): surface spellings the term normalizes, e.g. 007, 1e3, implicit vs ? vs ?? hole flavor, quoted labels, unknown infix operators (which now elaborate as stuck applications rather than evaluating to their last operand as multi-holes do).

Copy semantics are documented on the type: id-bearing fields drop on copy, value-meaning fields persist.

All other roundtrip gaps filled exploit existing structure rather than new fields. A representative trick: whether a sum type had a leading + is encoded by collected id count, as a leading-plus parse absorbs the separator ids, yielding n ids for n variants, while a bare binary sum carries only the n-1 separators; evaluator-built sums (single id) print bare, which reparses to the same type. Similarly, middle-completion hole ids derive from the tile id instead of being stored.

## Preserved property + fuzzing

The roundtrip property is enforced by a QCheck fuzzer driving Perform.go with random insert/move/destruct sequences from the empty buffer, sampling the actual editor-reachable domain, which parser based generators would undersample (rule tiles only form inside cases; deleted openers, standalone |/=> tokens, some grout cases are edit-reachable only). Also added a corpus and shrunk-counterexample regression suites.

What's compared: canonical completion yields a deeply complete segment whose parse prints back with identical text and piece sequence (tile ids, labels, shards, secondary), modulo a canonical quotient (grout (ephemeral by design), and mold sorts). Spelling, shapes, and precedences compare strictly.

Measured on the fuzzer (5 seeds, 290 states): the grout quotient earns its keep on placement, not ids — grout lands where the parsed term doesn't reproduce it in ~23% of reachable states (dangling boundary grout, stray grout glommed through MakeTerm), while ids agree whenever placement does. (The 4 id-only exceptions traced to the printer minting fresh ids on multihole id shortfalls; padding is now derived, so printing is a pure function of the term.)

The decision to quotient grout ids & sorts is pragmatic; there are currently a number of edge cases, some of which have been addressed, but i think the move it towards making both of these dervied; this is already underway for grout on the virtual-grout branch. If we don't decided to make these derived, we could add more annotations to avoid the need to quotient. In any case you can currently roptionally un the fuzzer with the quotient disabled enumerates to exactly the disagreement states derivation or annotation must handle.

An example of an outstanding sort issue: type : then ]. The editor molds the orphan ] at Typ — the caret sits on the typ side of the :. but canonical completion places the missing [ at the start, reading the state as [? : ?] (an Exp list whose element is the ascription, not ? : [?]), so the reprint derives the ] at Exp. 

Other known generator limitations: it fuzzes single-char insertion, char-wise movement, and backspace (so no selections, backpack pick-up/put-down, or copy/paste) and excludes projectors (follow-up work).

## Later additions (building on the roundtrip)

- **Completion heuristics**: missing delimiters drop into the concave junction their deletion left when shape + sort + uniqueness agree (`let x 1 in 2` -> `let x = 1 in 2`; deleted `else`/`in`/case-bars restore in place); `fun x` over a let-body clips the arrow at the sort frontier instead of absorbing the let into the pattern; a backspaced delimiter's leftover prefix token (`i` for `in`) is completed in place, recorded as a partially-typed shard (`{present, prefixes}` mask) so the roundtrip still closes exactly; leading witnesses restore deleted form heads from their remnants (`le` -> `let`, mid-program); sort-aware symbolic witnesses complete `-` -> `->` and `=` -> `=>`; broken cases repair as one case (wrap/opener arbitration + rule walls), and rules are treated as case-content throughout — mid-entry `case foo |` keeps its `end` after the growing rule.
- **Scoreboard instruments** (Test_CompletionScoreboard, pinned): deletion-inverse restoration over a corpus — full-deletion, last-char-prefix, joint pair-deletion (restoration + delimiter-completeness), and acceptance-stability (applying one suggestion must not move the rest; 96/104 stable, shifts only on known jointly-interacting states). Every remaining miss is a documented accepted-inherent (e.g. `f(3 + f(4)` is byte-identical to a freshly typed wide paren).
- **Quiver chips**: completion suggestions render as interline signposts at their exact placements — a bubble on the line boundary with a ghost-caret pole pinning the insertion column — replacing the old end-of-line boxes. Pins follow the caret through semantically-free whitespace; typed prefixes render cut-out; colorways distinguish tab-territory (pale) from other-segment obligations (gold); at caret coincidence the real caret is authoritative and the chip's pole steps aside.
- **Discharge routes**: `ApplyCompletion(All | One(tile))` materializes the virtual completion into the buffer (caret preserved by id). Alt+M completes everything (replacing the old greedy Dump, now deleted); cmd/ctrl+click on a chip completes exactly that delimiter (pointer cursor while the modifier is held; unmodified clicks pass through to the editor); tab still puts down at the caret. Agent/composition flows materialize through the same engine.
- **TyDi delimiter suffixes**: the ghost suggestion survives on prefix states where completion consumed the token's statics entry (ci-free witness route), 1-char expectation-backed prefixes bypass the length gate (`-`/`=` get arrow completions), and suggestions come from the same witness recognition the engine uses — ghost and quiver agree by construction. Tab at `els` accepts to `else` instead of dropping a fresh delimiter after it.
- **Reassociation**: retyping a deleted keyword char mid-program re-pairs with its orphaned shards (rescan matches singletons only; the repair fallback now explodes remnants and tries the sibling scope); `deep_reassociate` is no longer a setting — reassociation is unconditional, and the harnesses run it (they previously silently didn't, hiding this bug class from every edit-derived test).
- **Formatting**: SpaceNormalize gains an opt-in canonicalize mode (mold-aware within-line respacing: `f (x)` -> `f(x)`, one space around infix ops, comments/linebreaks untouched) backing the new Spaces format level; format actions restore the caret via CaretPreserving (from #2231 — exact piece, else surviving predecessor, else ancestors). Printing is now a pure function of the term (pad_ids derives instead of minting).
- **Auto-reindent triggers**: paste re-indents the pasted lines (settled exact / unsettled uniform shift) and, like TyDi accept, destruct, and comment-toggle, runs the completion-triggered re-indent when a tile completes.
- **Indentation UX** (gated on a core setting, on by default): arrow movement skips leading whitespace (every line keeps one reachable position; clicks/selection stay char-exact); backspace at first-content inverts enter (indent + linebreak, one keystroke, one undo); Cmd+[/] indent/dedent lines from any position; Shift+Backspace dedents at the line-start boundary only.

## Removals

The backpack display is retired (the quiver is the completion display; the put-down mechanism and derived missing-shards machinery remain — internals renamed from "backpack" to missing_shards), along with `Dump`, the `deep_reassociate` setting, and the redundant NutMenu Docs toggle. Persisted settings blobs lose two fields, so browsers may see a one-time settings reset.

## Addendum

- A batch of fidelity fixes found by the fuzzer along the way, including the two closed issues above.
(cross-sort tiles in MakeTerm, crossed synthesized delimiters, adjacent-operator lexemes, typ-side incomplete forms, and more); #2373 remains outstanding.
- docs/segments.md documents the round-trip contract, the provenance fields, and the sort-quotient rationale with the example above.
- Possible future refinements, deferred: sort re-derivation as above; virtual grout (#2165) as the same derive-don't-store program applied to grout.
